question: Carbonsate GmbH operates a project in Otjiwarongo (Namibia) in which harvested bush biomass is chipped and stored in sealed underground chambers. For the alleged long-term storage of CO2, the company sells allowances on the voluntary market. At the same time, wood-fired power plants are classified in the EU as contributing to the energy transition and climate protection.

For example, a new thermal power plant in Chemnitz is expected to burn around 100 000 tonnes of wood per year from the end of 2027. Both approaches claim to produce climate benefits: in Carbonsate GmbH’s project, carbon is stored in the wood in the long term to prevent it being released; meanwhile, when wood is burned, the carbon in the wood is released directly as CO2.
This raises questions about the real climate footprint and the coherence of policy incentives. 1.

What does the Commission make of the sale of carbon removal certificates for the underground storage of biomass, in particular in terms of additionality, permanence, possible methane emissions, lifecycle assessment and double counting?
Does the Commission intend to develop its own certification methodology for this as part of the EU certification framework for carbon removals? What requirements will it lay down?
How does the Commission justify the fact that the storage of woody biomass is considered carbon removal, while burning that biomass is considered renewable and climate-friendly?
